title: One patient, four decisions
intro: Margaret Ellis, 72, takes warfarin. She falls at home and breaks her hip. Follow four of the twelve moments of her stay. In each one the AI suggests and a named person decides.

end.title: Twelve suggestions, twelve people's decisions.
end.text: The eight steps not shown work the same way: triage, imaging orders, a critical INR, medication reconciliation, the OR booking, a night-time alert, patient instructions and coding.

role.name: Maya Nakamura
role.title: registration clerk
role.text: You register patients. You see who they are and that they are registered, never why.

chapters.title: No orthopaedic bed
chapters.meanwhile: Since the call (steps 2–4): triage suggested CTAS 2, her hip X-ray and CT were ordered, and an INR of 3.8 was flagged. Each was suggested by the AI and decided by a nurse or physician.

role.name: Jordan Lee
role.title: bed manager
role.text: You decide for the whole hospital, but you see patients only as MRN and bed.

chapters.title: The discharge summary
chapters.meanwhile: Steps 6–8: the pharmacist caught warfarin with naproxen and a missing home medicine, the OR booking was stretched to the predicted 115 minutes, and a NEWS2 alert fired on her first night.

role.name: Dr. Victor Osei
role.title: orthopaedic surgeon, her attending
role.text: Only your signature makes the discharge summary part of her record.

chapters.title: 48 hours later
chapters.meanwhile: Step 10: the ward nurse signed her plain-language instructions: the warfarin diet and the wound red flags.

role.name: Vera Uchida
role.title: Surgery ward nurse
role.text: Escalations from her follow-up call come to you; the call itself never gives medical advice.

steps.caption: You don't take this call; the AI agent does. It checks her name, birth date and the last four health-card digits before it discusses anything.
The agent pre-fills her ED registration from the call, marked AI. Nothing is recorded until you press Confirm: one click instead of retyping, with your name on it.
She needs an orthopaedic bed and Orthopedics is full. The rule engine raises this exception from live bed data; no model decides that there is a problem.
The AI writes the briefing from the engine's facts only: occupancy, who is boarding, who is ready to leave. It explains the problem; it moves no bed.
Your decision: early discharge rounds on Surgery, where two patients are ready to go. Tasks go to their teams, and the first bed they free is hers.
You see her only as MRN 40720001 in a Surgery bed. Her name, reason for admission, vital signs and orders are hidden: a bed decision doesn't need them.
The AI drafted her discharge summary. Every line names the record it came from (an order, a result, a note), so you check sources rather than memory.
Lisinopril appears in a note but in no order. The validator marks it red and blocks your signature: the AI cannot slip an unsupported medicine into her record.
You remove it, the validator checks again, and you sign. The summary is final under your name; the draft never was part of her record.
Two days home, the AI calls her with questions from her signed instructions. "The gauze is soaked through": a rule, not the model, escalates at once.
Her escalation tops your queue, in her own words. You call her back and record it. By design the call would rather over-escalate than miss a wound problem.
